summary: A framework document that describes and motivates Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) methods, which stop nodes on the same IP link from spoofing each other's addresses. It complements ingress filtering with finer-grained checks; specific methods are defined elsewhere.

plainLanguage.summary: SAVI checks whether a packet's source address belongs to the host attachment that sent it. This adds per-address checks on a link, alongside broader ingress filtering between networks.

questions: how to prevent ip source address spoofing on a link
how does source address validation improvement work
what is a savi protection perimeter
subtitle: A framework for checking that hosts use legitimate source addresses on a shared link.

tldr.problem: IP source addresses can be chosen by the sending host, so a host on a link can impersonate another address. Ingress filtering checks at network-prefix scale rather than for individual hosts.
tldr.mechanism: A SAVI instance learns legitimate addresses from assignment traffic, binds each address to a link-layer property of the host's attachment, and checks packets against that binding.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7039 is a framework document that describes the SAVI design. Specific SAVI methods are defined in other documents.

today: RFC 7039 is an Informational framework published in October 2013. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; specific SAVI methods are described in other documents.

sections.title: Why Validate Source Addresses
sections.content:
Hosts and network devices use an IP source address to identify where a packet came from and where replies should go. The Internet architecture does not itself prevent a sender from choosing a different source address, which can enable impersonation, concealment, or malicious redirection.

Ingress filtering checks whether the source prefix is routed to the network from which a packet arrived. SAVI complements that approach by checking individual IP addresses on a shared link, so one host cannot use another host's address.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can put an untrue source address in a packet. SAVI checks addresses between hosts on the same link, at a finer level than network-wide ingress filtering.

sections.title: Identify, Bind, and Enforce
sections.content:
SAVI is network-based and does not require special support from hosts. A SAVI instance first identifies which source addresses are legitimate by monitoring address-assignment traffic. It then binds each address to a binding anchor, a link-layer property of the host's attachment that can be checked on packets and should be harder to spoof than the IP address.

Finally, the instance enforces the binding by checking that each packet's source address matches the anchor associated with it. SAVI can run in a default router or in a switch between hosts and the router. Placing it close to the host makes it more likely to observe and check the host's traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: SAVI learns which addresses a host may use, links them to a property of its network attachment, and checks later packets against that link. Placing the check near the host helps prevent traffic from bypassing it.

sections.title: Assignment Methods and Binding Anchors
sections.content:
SAVI variants must account for how hosts receive addresses. The framework discusses DHCP, IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC), Secure Neighbor Discovery, IKEv2, and combinations of these methods. Separate variants can keep deployments using one assignment method simpler.

Possible binding anchors include an interface's EUI-48 or EUI-64, an Ethernet switch port, a wireless security association, a cable-modem customer relationship combined with a link-layer address, or a tunnel to one host. Their strength varies: an EUI can be spoofed, and a switch port may connect to more than one host.
sections.plainLanguage: SAVI needs to understand how a host received its address and what attachment information can identify that host. Some anchors, such as an interface identifier, are easier to spoof than others.

sections.title: Scaling, Recovery, and Prefix Setup
sections.content:
When several SAVI switches share a link, they could store duplicate bindings. The framework describes a protection perimeter: switches validate packets as they enter the perimeter, then avoid repeating the same checks inside it. This reduces duplicated state, but hosts attached to ports without enforcement can still use spoofed addresses.

A binding may be missing if address-configuration traffic is lost, a device restarts, or the topology changes. SAVI can create a binding reactively after excessive drops, but first checks whether the address is unique; the check depends on the assignment method. For SLAAC it uses Duplicate Address Detection; for DHCP it queries the DHCP server.

Before creating bindings, the SAVI device needs the allowed address prefixes. The RFC describes manual configuration, Router Advertisement snooping, and DHCP Prefix Delegation snooping, and recommends manual configuration in partial deployments because control messages can be spoofed.
sections.plainLanguage: A protection perimeter limits repeated checks and saves memory, but traffic entering through unprotected ports remains a risk. SAVI can rebuild a missing binding after it verifies that the address is unique on the link.

sections.title: Limits of Source Validation
sections.content:
SAVI mitigates some use of forged IP addresses but does not prove ownership in a strong sense. If a binding anchor is shared or weak, a host may still forge addresses. The RFC says cryptographic authentication is needed when strong security is required.

Placing SAVI close to hosts can expose the SAVI devices themselves. The RFC advises against putting SAVI functionality in physically exposed devices that an attacker could replace, and cautions against deployments across administrative boundaries that require trusting devices on the other side.
sections.plainLanguage: SAVI relies on the strength and exclusivity of its binding anchors, so it does not provide strong proof of address ownership. Its own devices must also be protected from replacement or misuse.

items.title: Identify
items.text: Learn which source addresses are legitimate by monitoring assignment traffic.

items.title: Bind
items.text: Associate each address with a host attachment anchor.

items.title: Enforce
items.text: Check that packet source addresses match their bindings.
